I'll just spend a few minutes explaining how the reserve works and what you can see today. Before describing the individual features of this nature reserve welcome, it is useful to understand the overall sequence. The information for the nature reserve welcome follows the order in which most people encounter the site or activity, beginning with orientation and moving towards more specialized areas. Knowing that sequence will make the later directions and choices in the nature reserve welcome easier to follow. First, a few important rules. We want everyone to enjoy the reserve, but there are a couple of things we don't allow. I'm afraid dogs are not permitted anywhere on the reserve, even on a lead, because they disturb the ground-nesting birds. And although the lake looks inviting, swimming is strictly forbidden. The water is much deeper and colder than it appears. You are very welcome to cycle but only on the marked trails, not on the narrow footpaths. Photography is positively encouraged, and picnicking is fine in the designated area near the car park. Some arrangements connected with the nature reserve welcome may operate differently during the present program. During the nature reserve welcome, listen for the difference between a permanent feature and something available only at a stated time. Where a condition in the nature reserve welcome is fixed, it will be presented as a rule. Where there is flexibility, it will be described as a recommendation. Now let me tell you about the reserve itself. Blackwater covers around 200 hectares of wetland and forest. It was established in 1987, originally to protect a single rare species of dragonfly, but today it's home to more than a hundred kinds of bird. The most popular attraction is our bird hide, which overlooks the main lake. From there in winter you can often see large flocks of geese that migrate here from Scandinavia. As the nature reserve welcome continues, a shorter route may reach the same principal areas. Within the nature reserve welcome, a change to a minor detail does not necessarily alter the main program. If an alternative becomes necessary during the nature reserve welcome, wait for the full announcement before moving, because the first place mentioned may be the one that is no longer available. Do not try to memorize every detail of the nature reserve welcome at once. The most important instructions will return when they become relevant. For now, concentrate on where the activity begins, which direction or sequence applies, and the point at which you may need to make a choice or ask a member of staff. If you follow the Blue Trail, it takes you through the ancient woodland, where some of the oak trees are over 400 years old. The Red Trail is longer and leads to the Observation Tower, which gives you a spectacular view across the whole reserve. Do allow about two hours if you want to complete it. A final way to follow the nature reserve welcome is to separate descriptive information from an instruction that requires action. Descriptions help you build a mental map, whereas instructions tell you when to move or decide. Keeping those functions separate will prevent an interesting detail from being mistaken for a change to the program. Our visitor center, just behind me, has a small cafe and a shop selling maps and guidebooks. There's also an exhibition explaining how the wetland is managed. Entry to the reserve is free, but we rely on donations, so please give generously if you can. Finally, the reserve closes at dusk, so please make sure you've returned to the car park before the gates are locked. Enjoy your visit and do come and find me if you have any questions. If you become uncertain during the nature reserve welcome, pause at the next staffed point rather than following another group without checking. Explain the last location or instruction you clearly remember, and staff can reconnect you with the correct sequence. This is especially important when two activities begin near one another, or when a temporary diversion changes only one section of the route. The program is designed to allow questions, so asking for clarification will not make you miss the main activity. Some mechanisms are supported by direct observation, while others remain the best explanation available from indirect evidence. A conclusion should be as strong as the evidence allows, but no stronger. Keep that distinction in mind as the examples are brought together. The separate examples in the Desert Ecosystem Lecture can finally be organized around three questions, what conditions begin a change, which mechanisms sustain it, and what consequences appear later. In the Desert Ecosystem Lecture, returning to those questions will connect evidence gathered at different scales. The conclusion to the Desert Ecosystem Lecture will use that framework to connect the details without extending them beyond the available evidence. Deserts are also fragile, because plants grow so slowly, any damage takes a very long time to repair. One of the greatest threats is desertification, the process by which fertile land gradually turns into desert, usually as a result of human activities such as overgrazing by livestock. Climate change is expected to make many existing deserts even drier in the coming decades. A useful final check is to ask, what observation would make the present account of the Desert Ecosystem Lecture less convincing? Identifying such evidence keeps the explanation testable and reveals where future research would be most informative. It also prevents a plausible narrative from being treated as complete, merely because its separate examples fit together. Yet, deserts also offer opportunities. They receive intense sunshine, which makes them ideal locations for generating solar energy. And scientists study desert organisms in the hope of discovering compounds that could be used in medicine. Far from being empty wastelands, deserts are dynamic systems that deserve our protection. One final point about the Desert Ecosystem Lecture concerns the difference between a useful model and a complete explanation. A model selects the relationships that matter most for a particular question, so it can be informative even when it leaves out local variation. Problems arise when that simplification is forgotten, and a result from one scale is treated as a rule for every case. The evidence discussed here should therefore be read with its conditions attached. The period observed, the population or material studied, the method used, and the uncertainty that remains. Those conditions do not weaken the account. They show exactly where the conclusion is supported and where further observation would be needed. The answer is complete. Check your answers.
